entries.entity: O*NET 19-4043.00 detailed materials (geological technician tasks and work activities)
O*NET 19-4043.00 occupation profile and official scope

paragraphs: Adjacent occupations are compared by main object and output, and sampling, recording, quality review, analysis, and reporting often overlap: geological/hydrologic technicians support field and laboratory data; geodetic surveying focuses on control and coordinate results, mining/petroleum engineering on engineering methods and schemes, environmental science on monitoring and assessment, and hydrologists on process research and water resource problems. Duties and signing authority depend on the actual position and jurisdiction, and the occupation name does not automatically grant or exclude them.

Preface | The comparison below is organized in four columns: 'occupational direction — core work and outputs — key difference — what it is better suited to'. Sampling, testing, measurement, engineering design, and environmental assessment are often linked within the same project or institution, but linkage does not mean they are interchangeable; when choosing across directions, the methods, specifications, authorization, and responsibility boundaries of that direction must be learned anew.

The main objects differ, and tasks overlap: environmental scientists also sample, analyze, and perform quality checks, and engineers also review records and equipment; hydrologic technician tasks explicitly may include models and cost-benefit analysis. Adjacent occupations cannot be described as not carrying sampling quality or safety, and technicians cannot be described as never doing models or evaluation. Real projects define the interfaces, methods, and authorization.

Better suited to people who are willing to move between the laboratory, well bores, rivers and lakes, and other field sites, can strictly follow numbering, calibration, and recording rules, and retest and report when anomalies are found.

Core work and outputs: take part in geological, geophysical, geochemical, hydrologic, or marine surveys, reconnaissance, drilling, and logging projects according to the plan and collect solid or fluid samples; use laboratory instruments or testing equipment to prepare and test samples and compile, record, and enter data; measure and report flow rates and groundwater levels and maintain field equipment and install and recover sampling equipment; prepare notes, sketches, and geological maps or cross sections and record characteristics such as the pressure and temperature of wells or bore holes; prepare or review technical reports on sampling, testing, and data analysis; outputs are samples and testing data and field records and charts and reports (bounded combination of O*NET 19-4043.00 and 19-4044.00).
This occupation: Geological and Hydrologic Technicians (bounded combination of 19-4043.00 and 19-4044.00)

Key difference: geodetic surveyors take control network layout, observation, computation, and delivery of results as their object, and produce survey control results and coordinate and elevation data; this occupation takes samples, testing, and field data as its object and usually does not carry responsibility for control surveying or issuing survey results (but must collaborate with it and share the position datum).

Better suited to people who want to work on control surveying, instrument observation, computation, and delivery of results; this occupation leans more toward samples, testing, field data, and equipment maintenance.

Core work and outputs: lay out and observe control networks and process observation data, compute coordinates and elevations and prepare survey results and notes, and support engineering, cadastral, and resource surveys; outputs are survey control results, coordinate and elevation data, and survey reports.
Geodetic Surveyors (17-1022.01)

Key difference: mining and geological engineers take scheme design, resource evaluation, and engineering design as their object, and produce design schemes and professional conclusions; this occupation carries out sampling, testing, and recording according to the plan and does not carry responsibility for engineering design or reserve evaluation (but must provide data and sample support for them). Signing or acceptance authority is checked against the actual appointment, jurisdiction, and qualifications and is not granted by the occupational description itself.

Better suited to people who want to work on engineering design, calculation, judgment, and signing responsibility; this occupation leans more toward field sampling, testing, equipment, and data recording.

Core work and outputs: design extraction or exploration schemes and carry out resource evaluation and engineering calculations, assess geological conditions and risks, prepare designs and reports, and take signing responsibility for professional conclusions; outputs are design schemes and professional conclusions. Signing or acceptance authority is checked against the actual appointment, jurisdiction, and qualifications and is not granted by the occupational description itself.
Mining and Geological Engineers (17-2151.00)

Key difference: petroleum engineers take drilling, completion, and production scheme design and optimization as their object, and produce engineering schemes and professional conclusions; this occupation carries out sample collection, testing, and recording according to the plan and usually does not carry responsibility for oil and gas engineering design or operational decisions.

Better suited to people who want to work on oil and gas engineering scheme design, calculation, and optimization; this occupation leans more toward field sampling, testing, data, and equipment maintenance.

Core work and outputs: design drilling, completion, production, and stimulation schemes and carry out calculations and economic evaluations, assess operating risks, and prepare schemes and reports; outputs are engineering schemes and professional conclusions.
Petroleum Engineers (17-2171.00)

Key difference: environmental scientists and specialists take research and assessment of environmental monitoring, pollution, ecological, and resource problems as their object, and produce assessment reports and protection recommendations; this occupation takes sampling, testing, and field data as its object and usually does not carry responsibility for environmental compliance assessment or enforcement-related conclusions (but must provide data support for them).

Better suited to people who want to work on environmental monitoring, experimentation, assessment, and protection recommendations; this occupation leans more toward field sampling, testing, equipment, and data recording.

Core work and outputs: design and carry out environmental sampling, monitoring, and experimentation, analyze pollution, ecological, and resource problems and assess impacts, prepare assessment reports and protection recommendations, and take part in policy and public communication; outputs are monitoring and assessment reports and recommendations.
Environmental Scientists and Specialists (19-2041.00)

Hydrologists focus on hydrologic process research, models, and water resource and flood problems; hydrologic technicians may also take part in models, cost-benefit analysis, and real-time flood data. The difference is the actual research scope and the outputs they are responsible for, and modeling cannot be excluded or signing authority uniformly inferred from the name.
Better suited to people who want to work on hydrologic analysis, modeling, and water resource evaluation; this occupation leans more toward field observation, sampling, equipment, and data.

Core work and outputs: carry out hydrologic observation and analysis and build and calibrate hydrologic models, evaluate water resources and flood risk, and prepare analysis and evaluation reports; outputs are hydrologic analysis and evaluation conclusions.
Hydrologists (19-2212.00)

Transition | This page places adjacent positions side by side by 'object, output, and authorization level' to help you judge which kind of field sampling, testing, measurement, engineering design, environmental assessment, or hydrologic analysis position you want to invest in long term. Whichever direction you choose, what really determines whether you can take the job is the education, methods, specifications, authorization, and responsibility requirements of that direction, the ability to record the method basis, sample chain, quality control, and limitations clearly, and the willingness to take responsibility for data quality, field safety, and environmental and data compliance; interest questionnaires are only used to raise questions.
AI tools and review responsibilities

May 2025 OEWS covers U.S. wage and salary workers. The self-employed are outside the survey scope. Each SOC is a separate group. The survey does not give a combined wage series for this page title. May 2025 national medians: Geological technicians, except hydrologic technicians (19-4043): $53,350/year; Hydrologic technicians (19-4044): $64,790/year.
